You are a fresh critical reviewer. The BookMinder author has explicitly asked for an adversarial review of one of his own design decisions — he is genuinely unsure and wants alternatives considered, not deference. Repo /home/user/BookMinder, branch claude/bookminder-recall-5ite2s.

=== THE DECISION UNDER REVIEW (author-verbatim, voice-transcribed, 2026-08-12; [brackets] = transcription fixes) ===
"Oh, also note on the process with Red First... sorry, about the [commits] after Red, Green, and Refactor. This was my deliberate attempt to create a project record that that allows for easy... Rewinding, uh, between states. I I know it is absolutely irregular working pattern to be committing after the red state. But it is, like, uh, instruction following pressure. [Logging] practice later. Like, um, maybe this will become obvious, but I value process very highly. So I think this highly rigorous and disciplined process leads to better results than if models are trying to one shot solutions. So in the end in a project, we do not need... for a product, we would not need a granularity of [commits] on on on this [TDD] cycle level. But for the benchmark, it makes sense. Right? Normally, in a project, you would commit per feature. The... so... but if if we, like, we would then squash those commits, for example, or something like that. but forcing the model into the discipline. I I thought that was... I don't know. Useful."
And his challenge two days later: he questions whether the F1 detector family (red-first commit grammar, described below) "is a really necessary level. Here we're getting pretty meta recursive... There might be alternative ways to achieve project goals."

=== CONTEXT (read these) ===
- .coordination/eval-design.md — the benchmark design: trials = rewind repo to a checkpoint + story card + enforcement-ladder condition (C0 bare / C1 CLAUDE.md / C2 skill / C3 skill+hooks); T1 trajectory detectors over the candidate's commit DAG (F1 red-first-grammar: spec-introducing commit must fail, successor pass; F2 assertion-integrity; F3 minimality; F4 layering; F5 claim-vs-action over transcript; F6 refactor-honesty); grading = failure-modes × conditions matrix answering "how much harness enforcement does the discipline need".
- CLAUDE.md <tdd_discipline> + <git_workflow> — the current three-commits-per-cycle rule (RED/GREEN/REFACTOR), author-restored.
- .claude/skills/tdd-bdd/references/cycle-and-commits.md — how the compiled skill encodes the grammar.
- .coordination/threads.md lines ~26-28 (meta-goals incl. the corrected rationale record) and the "EVAL SCOPING DECISION" section.

=== THE QUESTION ===
Commit-after-RED currently serves FOUR distinct goals at once: (1) rewind substrate — checkpoints the benchmark can rewind to; (2) instruction-following pressure — an irregular pattern models must obey against their training prior; (3) process-forcing — the bet that granular discipline beats one-shotting; (4) measurement resolution — F1 grades trajectories by reading the commit DAG. Review whether one mechanism should carry all four, and whether each goal is best served this way. Known tension to adjudicate (coordinator's hypothesis — attack it too): F1 conflates instrument with subject — a candidate that breaks the commit grammar also degrades the record used to grade everything else, so measurement quality depends on candidate compliance.

=== ALTERNATIVES TO EVALUATE HONESTLY (extend the list) ===
(a) Harness-side shadow snapshots: the eval harness auto-commits/snapshots the tree after every tool call or test run (shadow branch, ref-log, or worktree copies) — rewind + measurement resolution guaranteed regardless of candidate behavior; commit-after-RED then becomes purely a discipline probe, gradable but not load-bearing. (b) Task-generation rewind actually needs only per-feature commits (eval-design rewinds to "the commit before story X") — interrogate whether cycle-level rewind points are needed AT ALL for trial generation, or only for grading. (c) Keep the grammar as C2/C3 skill+hook content but drop F1 as a detector (grade discipline via F5/F6 + transcript instead). (d) Keep everything as-is — steelman it: the grammar's irregularity is exactly what makes it a sensitive instruction-following probe (signal, not noise), it needs no harness machinery, and it tests what the author actually cares about (process fidelity under pressure); the product cost is zero because feature-squash-at-merge already reconciles it. (e) Anything else you find — e.g. hybrid: harness snapshots for measurement + grammar as graded behavior; or git-notes/tags instead of commits for cycle markers.
Also weigh REAL COSTS of the current design the author should see: tooling friction (CI gates, bisect, pre-commit hooks expecting green), the L-14 exception carve-outs already needed in CLAUDE.md, cognitive load on human contributors, and the meta-recursion the author smells — the benchmark measuring compliance with a rule whose main purpose is to make the benchmark measurable.

=== METHOD ===
Where a claim about the repo or eval design is checkable, check it (grep/read, cite file:line). Where you weigh alternatives, name the tradeoff concretely — no alternatives-theater: if an option is dominated, say so and why. Your recommendation must be falsifiable: state what evidence would overturn it. The author reads this personally: never hard-wrap prose, no praise, no meta-narration, lead with the verdict.

DELIVERABLE: .coordination/commit-after-red-review.md — verdict first (keep / modify / replace, one paragraph), then the four-goals decomposition with which mechanism serves each best, then alternatives adjudicated (incl. dominated ones), then costs of the recommended design, then "what would change this verdict". Commit ONLY that file (message: why — author-commissioned critical review of his own design), push -u origin claude/bookminder-recall-5ite2s (retry 4x backoff 2/4/8/16s network-only).

RETURN (max 10 lines): verdict one-liner, per-goal mechanism table in 4 lines, top cost of current design, what would overturn, commit SHA.

1	# BookMinder TDD-Discipline Eval — Design Sketch
2	
3	Status: draft, user-approved direction ("LGTM" on the pipeline, 2026-08-12). Companion to threads.md items 0b (eval), 00 (skill), and the mining pilot.
4	
5	## The question the eval answers
6	
7	Can an LLM agent *perform* (not merely describe) the author's BDD/TDD discipline — and how much harness enforcement does it need to keep doing so? Corollary: can it live within stock Claude Code (skill + hooks), or does the envisioned BDD pair programmer require a custom harness?
8	
9	## Pipeline: mine → compile → run → grade
10	
11	### 1. MINE (in progress — pilot on day-019 + day-016)
12	
13	Mining the session-transcript diary produces **two deliverable classes**:
14	
15	**A. Failure catalog** — incidents where the agent broke discipline, each with verbatim quote, location, user intervention, outcome, and a `detector_candidate`. The transcript shows what git cannot: the *rationalization* that accompanied the damage.
16	
17	**B. Philosophy & style corpus** — the author's design worldview as stated in dialogue: why TDD-as-process produces qualitatively different results, executable-truth reasoning, slicing/minimal-constraint thinking, London-school adaptations from typed Java (GOOS) to dynamic Python. Feeds the skill's motivation layer and anchors judge rubric items. (Schema v2 adds a `philosophy:` section per day-file; pilot ran with v1 where such material lands in `skill_rules`/`parked`.)
18	
19	Per-day YAML schema: `failure_modes` (name from controlled vocabulary / loc / quote ≤3 lines / what_happened / user_intervention / outcome / detectable_by / detector_candidate / rule_origin tag), `skill_rules` (rule / because / evidence / taught-once|repeated|needed-enforcement), `pairing_gems`, `philosophy` (v2), `parked` (the scope-creep parking lot).
20	
21	Reduce phase: deduplicate into a consolidated failure-mode taxonomy and a skill-rule candidate list.
22	
23	### 2. COMPILE
24	
25	Mining output compiles into three test-artifact types:
26	
27	- **T1 — trajectory detectors** (deterministic, pure git): scripts over the candidate's commit DAG. Examples: claimed-RED verification (check out spec-introducing commit, run the new test — must fail; successor commit must pass); AST-diff of spec files between commits to catch same-`it_`-name-with-weaker-assertion; `refactor:`-labeled commits re-verified by running pre-commit specs against post-commit code; impl edits with no preceding spec change; non-emptiness-guard presence on loop assertions.
28	- **T2 — dialogue detectors** (over the eval run's own full JSONL transcript — no scrollback lossiness in runs we control): claimed-vs-actual checks (agent asserts "tests pass" → verify a pytest tool call ran and passed), metrics quoted without tool-call provenance (fabrication flag), user-constraint dropped after N turns (instruction drift).
29	- **T3 — judge rubric items** (LLM judge, for the unmechanizable): slice choice, minimal constraints in specs, coupling of spec to contract vs implementation, naming-as-prose quality. Anchored by pairing_gems (positive) and mined failure quotes (negative). Judge output must cite quotes from the trial transcript.
30	
31	**The skill is itself falsifiable.** Every skill rule gets an ID; every T1/T2/T3 item references the rule ID it tests; a rule with no detector and no rubric item is unfalsifiable prose — it gets one or gets flagged. Coverage of the rulebook is a checkable property.
32	
33	### 3. RUN
34	
35	**Trial unit** = {repo checkpoint SHA, story card, condition}. The repo's own history supplies tasks: rewind to the commit before story X was implemented, hand the agent the repo + story card + condition's rule encoding. Difficulty tiers from the eras: greenfield story on the clean early tree; story on top of the lapsed suite; repair task ("fix the suite without being fooled by it").
36	
37	**Conditions — the enforcement ladder** (independent variable):
38	- C0: bare model, task only. Control rung — expected to one-shot; measures the baseline failure profile.
39	- C1: CLAUDE.md as-is. Tests prose constitution effectiveness (the author's historical failure mode).
40	- C2: BDD-style skill (extracted from the style guide + mining corpus).
41	- C3: skill + enforcement hooks (TDD-Guard-class: PreToolUse blocks impl edits without a failing spec; flags edits to existing `it_` bodies; commit-grammar checks).
42	
43	Low rungs are not expected to succeed — they are experimental controls that make the delta of each layer measurable.
44	
45	**Harness:** Claude Code run headless per trial in a container; capture final tree, commit DAG, and full JSONL transcript. Reference trajectories: for stories implemented during the gold-standard era, the author's actual commit sequence is the judge's reference.
46	
47	### 4. GRADE
48	
49	- T1+T2 run mechanically → list of *named* failure modes (vocabulary from mining; a violation is not "bad", it is "tautological-mock, day-013-class").
50	- Judge scores T3 per rule ID, quotes mandatory.
51	- Composite per trial: hard-gate on detectors / quality score from rubric / cost (tokens, turns, interventions).
52	- **Headline output: failure-modes × conditions matrix** — which harness rung eliminates which failure class. That is the custom-harness question answered with data.
53	
54	## Pilot acceptance criteria (current stage)
55	
56	The two-day mining pilot passes if: every failure_mode entry carries quote + loc + implementable detector_candidate; every skill_rule traces to evidence; off-schema observations land in `parked`; and spot-checking quotes against the source transcripts shows no fabrication. Pilot outputs land in scratchpad for user review before any repo commit (established review-first flow).
57	
58	## Compile/reduce policy (user's debug-build → optimized-build model, 2026-08-12)
59	
60	Mining output = the DEBUG BUILD: every claim fully back-referenced (loc, date, provenance type). The compile step later cuts the OPTIMIZED BUILD: executable rules stripped of provenance, split into THREE skills (user decision 2026-08-13): (1) tdd-bdd — generic discipline; (2) bookminder project-memory — Apple Books domain lore, fixtures; (3) pair-programming — conduct: design criticism, alternative-suggesting, expert-council invocation (channeling pretrained BDD/TDD expert simulacra), Socratic verification moves. Miners' schema predates the third skill: compile routes pairing_gems + conduct-shaped skill_rules to it (no cache invalidation mid-swarm).
61	
62	Contradiction resolution happens at compile, on the evidence base, ranked: (1) user-verbatim > user-paraphrase > agent-synthesis; (2) among user statements, later date overrides earlier (session numbering = chronology); (3) agent-era artifacts (YOLO period, post-downgrade Flash) never override an earlier user ruling. Output is a CONTRADICTION LEDGER — both quotes, dates, proposed resolution — for user ratification, never silent resolution. The ratified ledger also drives the gardening pass over stale README/CLAUDE.md.
63	
64	## Claims-verification design (proposed 2026-08-13, user prompted after stale-tense relay incidents; awaiting user go for first run)
65	Principle: a claim ships with its falsification procedure, as a requirement ships as a spec. (1) TYPED CLAIMS: workers emit present-tense repo assertions only as {claim, check} where check is an executable probe (grep/file:line/command+expected); untyped present-tense = source-time narrative by definition. (2) VERIFIER STAGE: standard post-fan-out stage runs every check against current tree, stamps VERIFIED@sha | STALE | FALSE — F5 detector pointed at our own pipeline. (3) FRESHNESS STAMPS: compile phase forbids present-tense claims in skills/backlogs/guide without verified_against: <sha>; stamps age visibly, re-verification = re-running checks. FIRST RUN (offered, not yet approved): sweep 24 YAMLs + canonical §5 for present-tense assertions → verified-residue.md, the stamped true repair backlog. KNOWN TRUST LIMITATION: validator audits quote: fields only — quoted-looking text in other fields (user_intervention etc.) is unverified corpus-wide; one fabricated instance already caught in day-018 by the repair agent.
66	
67	## Open design questions
68	
69	- Schema v2: `philosophy` section shape — verbatim quote + paraphrase + which skill/rubric element it feeds.
70	- Trial count & story selection: which stories × which checkpoints give the best difficulty spread for the cost.
71	- Judge model/effort and self-preference guards (same-model judging came out clean in this session's A/B/C experiment, but effort mattered).
72	- Hook implementation details for C3 (what exactly TDD-Guard-class hooks block vs. warn).
73	- Cross-model axis (the diary is 30% Gemini-era — failure modes may be agent-general; eval could later run non-Claude candidates).

1	# The cycle and its commits — RED, GREEN, REFACTOR
2	
3	## RED — earn the failure
4	
5	- **T-10** Run the specific new spec and observe it fail before writing any implementation, and say so explicitly — even when the defect was just observed in a real run on a real machine, because real-world feedback is not a licence to bypass RED; a spec that has never been executed in a failing state has not been shown to be capable of failing at all.
6	- **T-11** Any failure that tells you what to build next is legitimate RED — import errors, missing modules, and unfinished environment setup included; record the failure and let it drive the next minimal step rather than clearing it before declaring RED, because demanding an assertion failure specifically would skip the steps that build the package itself.
7	- **T-12** When a newly written spec passes on its first run, stop and treat that as a defect in the spec, not a completed step — a test that was never red proves nothing about the behavior it names.
8	- **T-13** To prove a new assertion on already-green code can fail, implement the opposite behavior on purpose, watch the red, then revert — adding an assertion that has never failed proves nothing about the assertion.
9	- **T-14** Commit after RED: commit the failing spec before writing any implementation — because the commit-per-phase record makes every cycle state rewindable, the log becomes the proof that a falsifier preceded the implementation, and the bet is rigorous process over one-shotting. RED commits and deliberately-red acceptance specs are the sanctioned exceptions to all-commits-passing.
10	
11	## GREEN — the minimum that passes
12	
13	- **T-15** Write the minimum production code that passes the failing spec: only the branch the red spec demands, never the symmetric or negated case — the opposite case is a separate scenario with no failing spec pulling it into existence, so it would ship untested.
14	- **T-16** When adding an element to working output, append to the existing expression rather than restructuring it in the same change — a rewrite silently alters output other specs already own, converting a feature addition into an unreviewed regression.
15	- **T-17** Run the full suite, then commit the passing spec plus minimal implementation immediately after GREEN, before starting any refactoring — refactoring on top of an uncommitted GREEN destroys the revertible checkpoint the cycle exists to create. Commit only what the red spec drove: read the staged diff and back out any production change no spec demanded before the commit lands.
16	
17	## REFACTOR — a phase, not an afterthought
18	
19	- **T-18** After every GREEN, explicitly ask whether to refactor and either name the duplication found or state that there is none, before starting the next behavior; if the refactor phase gets abandoned for a digression, return to it before the next story — a cycle left at GREEN is unfinished, and the next story buries the evidence.
20	- **T-19** Refactor the specs too, in their own commit — tests are code and decay exactly like implementation.

30	- **T-26** Run the suite and coverage after every single edit, combined into one command, not after a batch — batching hides which change broke or un-covered what and destroys the incremental commit boundary.
31	- **T-27** Before committing, run the whole gate explicitly — formatter, linter, type check, full suite, coverage — and show each output rather than claiming you ran it; run the full suite locally before every push, never using CI as the first place a change is exercised.
32	- **T-28** Never bypass a failing quality gate (skip flags, no-verify, silencing markers): the block is information about your workflow, so fix the cause and let the gate itself prove the fix. Treat tool warnings and "Skipped / no files to check" as part of the failing state — a gate that inspected nothing is a gap, never a pass.
33	- **T-29** Nothing is done until it has been executed and observed: before claiming a change is ready, run it — the documented command, the suite, the config, the migration — and report the command and its output. Reproduce a reported failure by running the project's own documented command before proposing a fix, verify locally before publishing, and confirm on the remote that a pushed change actually landed.
34	- **T-30** Treat a failing or empty test run as a fact about your own invocation until proven otherwise — activate the environment, retry, and read the retry's output before any conclusion that depends on it — because an unexamined tool error silently becomes a false premise for every downstream claim.
35	- **T-31** When a fix attempt does not change the observed symptom, revert it before trying the next hypothesis, and say out loud that it did not help — keeping inert fixes stacks unverified variables and later gets them documented as essential.
36	- **T-32** Undo a landed change with git revert, never by hand-reconstructing the earlier state — a hand-written inverse is unverifiable and loses the record that the change was deliberately undone; after a revert, grep the tree for the reverted mechanism rather than trusting the revert's range to have removed all of it.
37	- **T-33** Commit story-card and requirements changes on their own before touching any spec or implementation — separating what-we-want from how-we-did-it keeps the requirement revertible and citable from the implementation commit.
38	- **T-34** To establish what a codebase actually implements, run its suite and read the `--spec` output — never infer implemented scope from directory listings, module names, or summaries, because the executing suite is the only description of the system that cannot silently rot away from it.
39	- **T-100** Never claim the discipline produced an improvement — coverage gained, cost saved, code reduced — until at least one complete cycle has been executed and observed, and never compare stages that are not comparable: measuring a walking skeleton against a feature-complete predecessor measures scope, not method, so the numbers are meaningless rather than merely unverified.
40	- **T-98** A commit message may claim only what the staged diff does: read the diff of every file you are about to describe — including files changed by hand — before writing the message, because the log is an audit record and a message describing a different change destroys its value as one.

# Commit-after-RED: adversarial review

Commissioned by the author 2026-08-14 ("getting pretty meta recursive... There might be alternative ways to achieve project goals"). Reviewer: fresh agent, no stake in the prior design. Every repo claim below was checked against the tree at d33f4ae; citations are file:line.

## Verdict

**Modify.** Keep commit-after-RED as candidate-facing discipline — in CLAUDE.md, the tdd-bdd skill, and the C3 hooks — and keep a red-first detector. But demote F1 from measurement instrument to measured behavior: add harness-side snapshots as the eval's measurement substrate, define red-first process fidelity over the transcript timeline rather than the commit DAG, and score grammar-compliance (instruction-following) separately from red-first-in-time (process fidelity). The current design has two measurement defects the steelman cannot touch: F1's sensitivity co-varies with the experiment's independent variable (non-compliant low-rung candidates produce commit DAGs the T1 detectors cannot inspect, so exactly the rungs designed to fail are the ones where failures go undercounted), and F1 is forgeable (a one-shot implementation followed by selective staging yields a fully compliant DAG — commits order tree states, not authorship). Neither defect argues against the *rule*; both argue against renting the eval's instrument from the subject under measurement.

## The four goals, decomposed

| Goal | Current mechanism | Best mechanism | Finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Rewind substrate | cycle-level commits | per-feature commits (already required) + harness snapshots if finer replay is ever needed | Goal drops out. eval-design.md:35 rewinds trials to "the commit before story X was implemented" — story granularity. No trial tier starts mid-cycle. YAGNI, by the project's own constitution (CLAUDE.md:15). |
| 2. Instruction-following pressure | the grammar, stated at C1+ | same — unchanged | Holds. The irregularity is the probe's value: it opposes the training prior (models commit green), so compliance discriminates. Needs a compliance grader (F1a below), which is cheap. |
| 3. Process-forcing | the rule + C3 hooks | same rule; but its *measurement* function moves to snapshots | The bet ("rigorous process > one-shotting") is what the enforcement ladder tests — the rule is subject matter, correctly placed. The RED commit's one real mechanical contribution is freezing the spec baseline before implementation pressure exists; snapshots provide that baseline without candidate cooperation. |
| 4. Measurement resolution | F1-F6 read the candidate's commit DAG | harness snapshots + transcript; candidate DAG demoted to a claim, cross-checked | The load-bearing role fails twice — condition-correlated sensitivity and forgeability — detailed below. |

The author's own recorded premise — "for a product, we would not need a granularity of commits on this TDD cycle level. But for the benchmark, it makes sense" (threads.md:27) — is half true. The benchmark's *task generation* does not need it (eval-design.md:35). The benchmark's *grading* wanted it, and grading is precisely the function that should not depend on candidate behavior.

## The coordinator's conflation hypothesis, attacked both ways

**Where it overstates.** "Degrades the record used to grade everything else" is too broad. T2 runs over the harness-owned JSONL transcript — "no scrollback lossiness in runs we control" (eval-design.md:28) — and T3 judges the transcript and final tree. Neither depends on candidate commits. The final tree is always gradeable. And "grammar absent" is itself a clean top-line result for the discipline question at that rung, not a measurement failure.

**Where it understates.** The real defect is not that the record degrades — it is that it degrades *differentially by condition*, and condition is the experiment's independent variable. Every T1 example in eval-design.md:27 needs commit granularity: RED checkout-and-run, AST-diff of specs *between commits*, `refactor:` commits re-verified, impl edits with no *preceding* spec change. A C0 candidate that one-shots into one commit gives these detectors nothing to inspect, so T1-detectable failure modes are undercounted exactly at the rungs the design expects to fail (eval-design.md:43). The headline failure-modes × conditions matrix (eval-design.md:52) then shows low rungs cleaner than they were — biasing the enforcement-delta estimate, which is the one number the eval exists to produce. An instrument whose sensitivity is a function of the independent variable is not an instrument; it is a confound.

**The second defect: forgeability.** F1's check — "check out spec-introducing commit, run the new test — must fail; successor commit must pass" (eval-design.md:27) — verifies tree states, not authorship order. A candidate that writes spec and implementation together can stage the spec alone, commit (the checkout genuinely fails — the impl is unstaged), then commit the impl. F1 passes; the process was one-shot. T-14's claim that "the log becomes the proof that a falsifier preceded the implementation" (cycle-and-commits.md:9) is therefore wrong as stated: the log is a *claim* that a falsifier preceded the implementation. The only proof is the transcript — a pytest tool call observed failing before the first implementation-file edit. The harness already owns that record.

**A third, smaller problem: the gold references fail the grammar.** eval-design.md:45 uses the author's actual commit sequences as judge references for gold-standard-era stories. The mined corpus era has no commit-after-RED practice — the miners recorded its absence explicitly (v2/day-004.yaml:832, day-005.yaml:592, day-016.yaml:845, day-017.yaml:921, day-020-s2.yaml:649, day-021.yaml:1287), and only four RED-labeled commits exist in the whole history, all 2025-07-13..07-26 (1d1fb34, 32d784b, bd47589, 5125e9c). F1-as-instrument grades candidates by a grammar the reference trajectories do not exhibit. Scope F1 to conditions where the rule was stated, and keep judges from treating reference trajectories as grammar-normative.

## Alternatives adjudicated

**(a) Harness-side shadow snapshots — adopt, as complement not replacement.** Snapshot the tree after every tool call (or every test run), supervisor-side. Guarantees rewind and uniform measurement granularity across all conditions; enables replay-based RED verification (check out snapshot N, run the named spec) independent of any candidate claim. Concrete win for F2: without a RED commit, a weakened assertion never enters the DAG at all — the spec is first committed already-weakened at GREEN, so F2-over-DAG is structurally blind to the exact failure it was mined to catch; F2-over-snapshots sees the strong→weak transition. Implementation note: do it from outside the candidate's view (supervisor rsync/overlayfs or a detached GIT_DIR), *not* as a visible PostToolUse hook — a "bare model" C0 rung with snapshot machinery in settings.json is no longer bare, and the observer effect would contaminate the control. Serves goals 1 and 4 only; goals 2-3 stay with the rule.

**(b) Per-feature commits suffice for rewind — confirmed true.** eval-design.md:35 needs story-boundary checkpoints only; difficulty tiers (greenfield / lapsed-suite / repair) are all era- or story-level. Cycle-level rewind for trial generation is a need no current design element has. Goal 1 is not a justification for the grammar.

**(c) Keep grammar as C2/C3 content, drop F1, grade via F5/F6 + transcript — half right, and the wrong half is fatal.** The demotion instinct is correct; the deletion violates the design's own falsifiability principle: "a rule with no detector and no rubric item is unfalsifiable prose" (eval-design.md:31). C1-C3 state the rule, so something must grade adherence. Dominated by (e), which keeps a cheap deterministic compliance check and adds the transcript check (c) wanted.

**(d) Keep as-is — the steelman, honestly.** The probe value is real (goal 2 holds). No harness machinery needed. The product cost is smaller than the cost list in this review's commission suggests: pre-commit runs only ruff/mypy, not pytest (.pre-commit-config.yaml:15-31), so hooks never fight a RED commit; and outside-in ATDD already keeps a deliberately-red acceptance spec on main mid-feature by design (CLAUDE.md:124), so the bisect predicate and any CI-green-per-commit invariant are *already* conditional — commit-after-RED raises the frequency of red tree states, it does not introduce them. Feature-squash-at-merge reconciles the rest, as the author said. **Rejected anyway**: the steelman defends the rule and the probe, which the modify verdict keeps in full. It has no answer to the condition-correlated sensitivity or the forgeability of F1-as-instrument — those are properties of where the measurement lives, not of the rule.

**(e) Hybrid — the recommendation.** Snapshots (a) carry measurement; the grammar stays as graded behavior; F1 splits into F1a (DAG grammar compliance: does the commit sequence exhibit RED-fail/GREEN-pass — instruction-following signal, cheap, deterministic) and F1b (transcript red-first-in-time: a failing run of the new spec precedes the first implementation edit — process fidelity, ground truth). F1a-pass ∧ F1b-fail is itself a named failure mode — call it retro-staged-grammar, discipline-theater class — and it is exactly the F5 claim-vs-action pattern applied to commits: the DAG is a claim, the transcript is the action.

**(f) git-notes / tags as cycle markers — dominated, discard.** Notes and tags attach to existing commits: they checkpoint nothing (no rewind value), are even cheaper to fabricate post-hoc than a staged commit, and lack the one real mechanical property the RED commit has — freezing the spec baseline before implementation pressure exists. Named for completeness; no tradeoff worth weighing.

## Costs of the recommended design

1. **Harness engineering.** Snapshot capture plus a replay runner. One-time; adjacent to infrastructure the harness already has (it captures final tree, commit DAG, and full JSONL per eval-design.md:45). The genuinely new cost is reconciliation logic across three records — DAG, snapshots, transcript — and that logic *is* the F1a/F1b/retro-staged-grammar detector, so it is spent on signal, not plumbing.
2. **The prose tax stays.** Because the grammar stays, the L-14 carve-outs remain owed: CLAUDE.md:242 ("preserve working state (all tests passing)") still contradicts :127 and :235-238, :132 still says "second commit" for the third (contradiction-ledger.md:152-159), and the skill carries the exception clause (cycle-and-commits.md:9, SKILL.md:16). Under this verdict that price is paid knowingly for goals 2-3, not smuggled in under "the benchmark needs it."
3. **The meta-recursion dissolves rather than resolves.** Measurement no longer depends on the measured rule, so the circularity the author smelled — the benchmark grading compliance with a rule whose main purpose was making the benchmark gradable — is gone. What remains is ordinary self-reference: an eval of instruction-following must state instructions. That is legitimate and unavoidable.
4. **Human-contributor load is unchanged.** The grammar remains a repo rule. If that ever bothers, it becomes a pure product decision with zero eval entanglement — which is precisely the separation this design buys.

## What would change this verdict

- **Pilot data showing both defects are empirically absent.** Run 5-10 C0/C1 trials: if low-rung candidates produce granular commit DAGs anyway (masking rare) *and* no DAG-vs-transcript divergence appears (no retro-staging), keep-as-is wins on simplicity and the snapshot machinery is unearned weight. This is the cheapest decisive experiment and should run before building (a).
- **Snapshots proving infeasible or contaminating.** If the chosen runner cannot snapshot supervisor-side and a visible hook measurably perturbs candidate behavior (A/B one trial with and without), accept the confound, annotate the matrix cells it biases, and keep as-is.
- **The pending 2025 JSONL upload showing real intra-story rewinds.** If the author actually rewound to RED checkpoints mid-story in practice, goal 1 revives at cycle granularity and strengthens the grammar's standing — but does not restore F1-as-instrument, since forgeability is untouched by that evidence.
- **Scope shrinking to C2/C3 only.** Near-universal compliance at high rungs removes the masking confound; the demotion case then rests on forgeability alone, and F1b becomes a nice-to-have rather than a correction.
- **Replace — dropping the grammar entirely — would need evidence this review did not find:** C1-C3 compliance so uniform the probe discriminates nothing, or the author abandoning the process-forcing bet. Neither is in the record.
